1.pericope_label: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign: a boy king under his guardian, and the wives chosen for him

schools.summary: Gill insists the two wives were taken for the king and not for Jehoiada, who already had a wife, the king's aunt, besides sons, and was upwards of a hundred; he names Jehoadan as one of them and allows the other to be unknown.

Henry draws two lessons, that it is a happiness for the young to set out under the direction of the wise and good and especially prudent to take advice in marriage, and that men may go far in the external performances of religion by education and the influence of friends while having no inward relish of them.
Clarke works the arithmetic, that a boy hidden six years in the temple and seven at his accession can have been only a year old when his aunt secreted him.

Ellicott reads the verses against their parallel, noting the omitted date, the contraction of Jehoash to Joash and its probable meaning, the relative force of all his days, and the absence of the two wives from Kings, which carries instead the note about the high places; Delitzsch refers the repair that follows to his own commentary on Kings.

debates: For whom were the two wives taken? Gill argues at length that they were for the king, not for Jehoiada, who was aged and already married to the royal aunt, and that he proposed them once Joash came of age, having watched the mischief done when Jehoram married Athaliah; Henry assumes the same and makes it a model of prudence in the young; Ellicott notes only that the statement is absent from the parallel narrative and was doubtless drawn from another source.
outliers: Ellicott alone offers an etymology, that the name may mean Iahu is fire but more probably Iahu is a man.
Henry alone turns the arrangement into a warning, that foreign inducements may push men on to what is good who are not actuated by a living principle of grace in their hearts.
themes: a king of seven under a guardian
a marriage left to another man’s choice
all his days read relatively
obedience that lasted as long as its prop

4.pericope_label: Joash was minded to repair the house of the Lord: the slack Levites, the chest at the gate, and what was done with the surplus

schools.summary: Gill allows Jehoiada to be high priest, head of his course or chief of the priests concerned, and makes him in effect prime minister of state; on the sons of Athaliah he follows Kimchi in denying the usual identification.

Clarke explains the dilapidation from the pillaging under Joram and Athaliah, calls this the first general collection for repairing a house of God, and identifies the collection of Moses with the half-shekel poll-tax; Wesley observes that Jehoiada is called only the chief, not chief priest, and reads the breaking up of both the treasuries and the house.

Ellicott prefers restore to repair, treats the chronicler as paraphrasing an unclear account, reads the going out to the cities as his interpretation of the instruction in Kings, denies that the tax of Moses is the half-shekel poll-tax, and resolves the contradiction over the vessels by distinguishing what was done during the repairs from the accounting of the surplus; Delitzsch explains the breaking up of the great vessels on practical grounds and has the king, not Jehoiada, cause the new ones to be made.

debates: What is the collection of Moses? Clarke identifies it with the half-shekel poll-tax levied on every man from twenty years old upward and reckoned a ransom for their souls; Ellicott denies this outright, holding that the tax of Moses is not that poll-tax but a general designation of the moneys named in the parallel account.

Who were the sons of Athaliah that broke up the house of God? Ellicott takes them for Ahaziah and his elder brothers, young princes gratifying the queen’s hatred of the exclusive worship of Jehovah, and guesses that parts of the buildings were pulled down to make room for a temple of Baal; Wesley agrees, adding that they did it at her instigation and broke up both the treasuries and the house itself; Gill flatly refuses the identification, following Kimchi in making them sons of Athaliah by another man.

Who made the vessels from the surplus? Delitzsch has the king cause them to be made; Ellicott gives the act to Jehoiada. Ellicott then meets the further difficulty that Kings denies any such vessels were made at all, supposing the earlier writer reports what was done with the money while the repairs were in progress while the chronicler accounts for what was left at the end, and admitting that the appearance of contradiction suggests the didactic aims of the later historian.
outliers: Ellicott alone dwells on the metaphor of the thirteenth verse, where the work perfected is literally a bandage applied to it, an expression used again of the walls of Jerusalem and before that by Jeremiah of a national restoration.
Ellicott alone explains the substitution of the high priest’s officer for the high priest himself as made in the interest of a dignity that had grown as the monarchy receded into the past.
Ellicott alone remarks that the chronicler is fond of dwelling on how willingly the people gave in the good old time, doubtless by way of suggestion to his own contemporaries.
themes: a king more zealous than his priest
Levites who hastened not
a chest set outside the gate
a tax disputed between two readings
a bandage laid upon the work
a surplus turned into vessels

15.pericope_label: But Jehoiada waxed old, and was full of days when he died: the princes turn the king, and Zechariah is stoned in the court

schools.summary: Gill reads the sending of prophets as clemency exercised before wrath, makes the Spirit upon Zechariah the spirit of prophecy, and notes that Joash remembered not the kindness by which he had been preserved and enthroned.

Henry diagnoses the apostasy rather than narrating it: the king had never been sincere but complied with the man who helped him to the crown, so that when the wind turned he turned with it; and he insists that in the most degenerate times God left not himself without witness, so that those who perish are inexcusable.

Clarke says Jehoiada had in fact been king, gives the Targum's fuller scene of incense burnt to an idol on the day of expiation, and traces how quickly the dying imprecation was answered; Wesley supplies the princes' pretext about journeys to Jerusalem, places the prophet in a desk of the priests' court, and reports the Jewish reckoning of seven transgressions in one.

Ellicott canvasses the physiology of a hundred and thirty years, reads the obeisance as the asking of a boon, objects to the rendering groves, observes that the priest is an epithet of Jehoiada and not of his son, and identifies the murder with the one Christ names; Delitzsch agrees on that identification and on the wrath being the Syrian invasion, and notes that the king did not venture to deny the princes their request.

debates: Is an age of a hundred and thirty credible? Ellicott canvasses the physiology, reporting a modern limit of about a hundred and five with one academician allowing half a century beyond it, and concludes the age is not impossible, though an error of transcription is not impossible either.

What did the princes ask for? Ellicott reads the obeisance as the asking of a boon whose nature the next verse makes plain, the royal sanction of the idolatrous forms they hankered after; Delitzsch says the request is nowhere stated but may be gathered from what they did, and that the king did not venture to deny them; Wesley supplies the pretext, that they asked relief from journeys to Jerusalem and the liberty of the high places, knowing they could then worship idols undisturbed.

Is this the Zacharias whom Christ names? Ellicott holds there is little doubt of it and suggests Barachias may have been the father and Jehoiada the grandfather; Delitzsch agrees and calls it the last prophet-murder the Old Testament narrates, both noting that the father named in the Gospel is not Jehoiada.
outliers: Wesley alone supplies the sting of the burial, that the little religion Joash had was all buried in Jehoiada’s grave.

Ellicott alone guesses that the prophet’s words had been represented to the king as treasonable, the Syrian threat perhaps already in the air, so that it would be easy to allege his wish was father to his thought.
Ellicott alone sets the dying imprecation against the prayer of Stephen, finding it in keeping with a dispensation that exacted blood for blood.

Wesley alone reports the Jewish reckoning of seven transgressions in one act, a priest, a prophet and a judge killed, innocent blood shed, and the court, the Sabbath and the day of expiation polluted.
themes: a regent buried among the kings
a king who turned with the wind
prophets sent and not heard
a prophet stoned in his father’s court
a dying prayer that was also a prophecy

23.pericope_label: And it came to pass at the end of the year: the Syrians destroy the princes, and Joash is slain on his bed

schools.summary: Gill marks the speed of the fulfilment, says the Syrian force consisted but of few, and notes that the invaders departed once they had got what spoil they could.

Clarke observes that neither assassin was a Jew and complains that kings have long made confidants of foreigners to their cost, takes the burdens for the Syrian tribute, and laments the loss of the midrash this verse cites, as Trogus Pompeius was lost to his abridger; Wesley reads the plural sons at face value, inferring that Zechariah's brothers were killed too, and makes the burdens the judgments by Syrians and sickness alike.

Ellicott works the military detail of a small detachment routing a large force, refuses to read the great diseases as battle wounds, treats the plural sons of Jehoiada as rhetorical rather than a transcriber’s slip, and argues from the names of the assassins’ mothers that the chronicler used a source other than the canonical book of Kings.

debates: What were the great diseases Joash was left in? Ellicott refuses to take them for battle wounds, since the text never says the king was wounded, and makes the word, which occurs here alone, mean pains or suffering, so that either calamity brought on the sickness or the invasion found him already prostrate; Wesley passes over the question and reads the murder as vengeance for innocent blood.

Why does the text say the sons of Jehoiada? Ellicott notes that the Greek and the Vulgate correct the plural to a singular, meaning Zechariah, and holds it more probably rhetorical than a transcriber’s slip, the point being not the conspirators’ motive but that their deed was a judgment on the king; Wesley takes the plural at face value and infers that Joash had killed the prophet’s brothers as well.

What are the burdens laid upon him? Clarke suggests the tribute exacted by the Syrians, though some think the sums amassed for the temple; Wesley makes them the judgments by Syrians and by sickness; Ellicott offers a threatening prophecy used collectively, or else a tribute, and rejects the reading suggested in the Hebrew margin as wholly improbable.
outliers: Clarke alone turns the nationality of the assassins into a political complaint, that foreigners should be banished from the person of a sovereign by strong and efficient laws.
Clarke alone laments the lost original behind the citation, comparing the forty-four volumes of Trogus Pompeius which survive only in the abridgment that caused their destruction.
Ellicott alone names and refutes two commentators on the mothers’ epithets, calling one incorrect and the other’s explanation fancy determined by prejudice.
themes: a judgment within the year
a great host routed by a small company
a sickness the text does not explain
a king buried outside the royal sepulchres
a source other than the book of Kings
